0. Objectives & the 5 Study-Check Questions

ObjectiveWhere

Ask these about every urinalysis (from the study guide)
  1. Can I trust this specimen? (collection, contamination, delay)
  2. What does each test measure?
  3. What does an abnormal result NOT prove?
  4. Where is it coming from? glomerulus, tubule, interstitium, or lower tract
  5. What is the best next test?
For exam cases add: does the pattern fit glomerular, tubular, interstitial or lower-tract disease, and does it show altered filtration, kidney damage, structural disease, or more than one?
Source conflictsWhere the Brick and the study guide disagree, I use the more accurate version and tag it corrected. Items I added that are in neither source are tagged beyond source. The study guide says not to spend much time on: drug-related urine colors/odors, rare crystals, glitter cells, exact reference ranges for every analyte, eGFR equation math, 24-h endocrine urine studies. Urine Na/osm, FENa, AKI/CKD staging come later with their disorders.

1. Key Tests for Early Kidney Disease

  • Early kidney disease is usually asymptomatic. Labs detect it two ways: (1) a decline in GFR (↑serum creatinine / ↓eGFR) or (2) abnormal substances in the urine (protein, RBCs, WBCs, casts, crystals).
  • Urinalysis + microscopy are the key screening tests (“a low-tech, low-cost renal biopsy”). Imaging then refines the diagnosis (§6). Renal biopsy is the definitive tissue test.
  • Urine quantification: spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) detects/quantifies albuminuria (earliest sign of diabetic kidney disease); spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (PCR) estimates total protein. The dipstick is too insensitive for early albuminuria.

Is the specimen reliable?

IssueKnow
Random specimenRoutine screening. First-morning specimen is more concentrated (useful for protein, nitrite, microscopy; avoids dilution).
Midstream clean-catchPreferred for urine culture (less contamination).
CathetersDon't sample from a chronic catheter drainage bag; use the sampling port with sterile technique.
Many squamous epithelial cellsGenital/distal urethral contamination. Bacteriuria + squamous cells = uninterpretable → recollect a clean-catch.
Delay in processingBacteria multiply, pH rises (alkaline), cells lyse, casts degrade.
ChildrenInfants concentrate poorly; bagged specimens are very prone to contamination; catheter/suprapubic for cultures. Congenital obstruction may present as infection or hydronephrosis.

Three layers of a urinalysis

ComponentWhat it gives
Gross appearanceColor, clarity. Useful, rarely diagnostic. Yellow normally; darker/lighter with concentration. Red/brown = heme: RBCs (hematuria), free Hb (hemoglobinuria) or myoglobin (myoglobinuria).
Dipstick (screen)Blood, protein, leukocyte esterase, nitrite, glucose, ketones, pH, specific gravity (+ bilirubin/urobilinogen). Semi-quantitative: 0, 1+, 2+...
Microscopy (sediment)Centrifuge → resuspend pellet → count cells/casts/crystals per high-power field (HPF).

2. Estimating GFR: SCr, eGFR, Creatinine Clearance, BUN

GFR benchmarks

  • Normal at ~20 years: 120–130 mL/min/1.73 m², falling ~10 per decade of age. Rule of thumb: don't worry until <90. The 1.73 m² denominator indexes to body surface area.
  • Quick bedside estimate (no kidney disease): GFR ≈ 140 − age.
  • A persistently reduced eGFR (not one value) supports chronic loss of filtration.

Serum creatinine (SCr)

  • Product of muscle catabolism; freely filtered, not reabsorbed, minimally secreted (10–15% is secreted by tubules) → it slightly overestimates GFR. Higher SCr = lower GFR.
  • Muscle mass confounds it: higher in young > old, male > female, meat-eaters > vegetarians, weightlifters/high lean mass. Low SCr with low muscle mass (elderly, cachexia) can hide real kidney disease.
  • Because of this variation, one SCr is a poor measure of GFR; use trends and eGFR.
  • beyond source GFR and SCr are inversely related and nonlinear: halving the GFR roughly doubles steady-state SCr. In AKI SCr lags the injury, so a normal SCr early doesn't exclude AKI.

Three ways to estimate GFR

MethodHowStrengths / limits
Serum creatinineSingle blood value (ref ~0.6–1.4 mg/dL in the Brick; ranges vary by lab)Cheap; best for trends; influenced by muscle mass, age, sex, diet
eGFR (CKD-EPI)Equation using SCr + age + sex (lab/online calculators). No need to memorize the math.Routine standard; reported by labs; better than SCr alone. Still an estimate (extremes of muscle mass, rapidly changing function)
Creatinine clearance (CrCl)CrCl = (UCr × V) / PCr, timed (usually 24-h) urine collection"Most accurate" of the three but cumbersome (collection errors); overestimates true GFR (tubular secretion)

beyond source Worked example: UCr 90 mg/dL, 24-h urine 1,440 mL (V = 1 mL/min), PCr 1.0 mg/dL → CrCl = 90×1/1.0 = 90 mL/min. (Inulin clearance is the true gold standard but is a research test.)

BUN

  • Serum urea (normal ~7–20 mg/dL); less useful than SCr because urea is made in the liver from protein.
  • ↑BUN without ↓GFR: high protein intake, GI bleed, catabolic states, corticosteroids. ↓BUN without ↑GFR: low-protein diet, liver disease.
  • beyond source BUN:Cr >20 suggests prerenal azotemia (urea reabsorbed with water in volume depletion); covered with AKI.

3. Urine Appearance & the Dipstick

Dipstick: what each pad means

PadInterpretationCaveat (what it does NOT prove)
BloodDetects hemePositive without RBCs on microscopy = hemoglobin (hemolysis/transfusion reaction) or myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis), not true hematuria
ProteinAnionic proteins, i.e. mostly albuminMisses cationic proteins (e.g. light chains of myeloma) and low-level albuminuria → need urine electrophoresis/light-chain assay or ACR
Leukocyte esteraseEnzyme from neutrophils/macrophages = WBCs presentNot specific for bacterial infection
NitriteBacteria that reduce nitrate (E. coli, Enterobacter, Proteus, Klebsiella)Negative doesn't exclude UTI (e.g. Enterococcus doesn't make nitrite)
GlucoseFiltered load > reabsorptive capacityCan occur with normal blood glucose if proximal reabsorption is impaired (Fanconi, SGLT2 inhibitors beyond source)
KetonesFasting/starvation, diabetic ketoacidosiscorrected The strip reacts mainly with acetoacetate; routine strips do not reliably detect β-hydroxybutyrate (the Brick lists both)
Bilirubin / urobilinogenHeme metabolites. Conjugated bilirubin (water-soluble) is filtered when diverted into blood by biliary obstruction or liver dysfunctionUnconjugated bilirubin is protein-bound and not filtered
pHSee belowInterpret with systemic acid-base status and infection
Specific gravityConcentration; correlates with osmolalityReflects water balance, not just kidney disease

Urine pH (normal 4.5–8, varies with acid-base status)

Low (<5)High (>7)
Extrarenal acidosis (lactic, DKA, glycol ingestion): kidney appropriately excretes acid
RTA types 2 and 4 (proximal and hyperkalemic) per the Brick		Systemic alkalosis (vomiting, bicarbonate/antacids)
Struvite ("infection") stones: urease-producing Proteus etc. alkalinize urine
Distal (type 1) RTA: high urine pH despite systemic acidosis (can't secrete H⁺)
Old/delayed specimen
Key ideaA normal kidney facing acidosis makes acid urine. An alkaline urine in a patient who is acidotic = the kidney is the problem (distal RTA). Link to your acid-base guide.

Specific gravity

UrineSGOsmolality
Isotonic (isosthenuria; seen when concentrating ability is lost)1.008–1.009~280 mOsm/kg
Dilute (after water load, DI)<1.003~100
Concentrated (water deprivation, dehydration)~1.035~1220
  • Desert wanderer → high SG. Persistently fixed ~1.010 suggests tubular/chronic kidney damage beyond source. Infants concentrate poorly.
  • Glucose: spills when serum glucose exceeds roughly 180 mg/dL in a diabetic with normal tubules (the Physiology guide used ~200 as the threshold; same concept).

4. Hematuria, Pyuria, Proteinuria, Crystalluria & ATN

Hematuria

  • Causes: stones, infection, bladder/renal cancer, glomerular disease, lower tract (cystitis, prostatitis).
  • Normal (isomorphic) RBCs → non-glomerular (stone, tumor, infection, lower tract). Dysmorphic RBCs (acanthocytes/donut shapes from squeezing through a damaged GBM) → glomerular bleeding. RBC casts are pathognomonic for glomerulonephritis.
  • Dipstick "blood" without RBCs → hemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis).
Normal RBC (left) vs dysmorphic RBCs (right) — glomerular bleeding

Pyuria

  • WBCs in urine: UTI (neutrophils), interstitial nephritis (eosinophils may be seen), renal TB, stones. Leukocyte esterase = WBCs present, not necessarily bacterial infection.
  • To separate UTI from inflammation, look for bacteria (nitrite, microscopy). Pyuria with negative nitrite: UTI still possible (e.g. Enterococcus); also consider noninfectious/atypical causes (AIN, TB, stones).
  • WBC casts can only form in the kidney → pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis.
Neutrophils (black arrows) and bacteria (white arrows) in UTI
WBC cast — intrarenal inflammation

Proteinuria

  • Some protein is normal (Tamm-Horsfall protein, made by tubules), but dipstick-positive proteinuria is almost always disease. Heavier (3+–4+) = more likely glomerular; 4+ usually nephrotic-range.
  • Dipstick detects albumin; urine albumin is both an early and (in large amounts) a late marker of glomerular disease. Early diabetic kidney disease needs a microalbumin/ACR test.
  • Light chains (myeloma) are cationic → dipstick can be negative → urine electrophoresis/light-chain assay.
  • Persistent proteinuria = kidney damage; transient proteinuria occurs with fever, exercise, physiologic stress.
  • Concept (types): glomerular (albumin leaks through damaged barrier), tubular (failure to reabsorb filtered small proteins), overflow (excess production, e.g. light chains).
  • Don't use the dipstick alone to judge severity or type: quantify with ACR/PCR.

Crystalluria

Crystals can be normal in concentrated urine, but also hint at stones or drug crystallization. Four to know:

CrystalShapeUrine pHAssociation
Calcium oxalateEnvelope (dihydrate); dumbbell/needle (monohydrate)VariableMost common stone. Monohydrate needles: ethylene glycol poisoning beyond source
Struvite (Mg-ammonium-phosphate)Coffin lidAlkalineUrease-producing infection (Proteus), "infection stones"
Uric acidRhomboid (varied)AcidicGout, leukemia, tumor lysis, high uric acid
CystineHexagonalAcidic (insoluble)Pathognomonic for cystinuria (rarest)
Calcium (dihydrate) — envelope
Struvite — coffin lids
Uric acid — rhomboids
Cystine — hexagons

Acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

  • Intrarenal AKI from toxic or ischemic (hypoxic) tubular cell death.
  • Microscopy is the clue: muddy-brown (coarse granular) casts = degenerated tubular epithelial cells, plus renal tubular epithelial (RTE) cells singly, in sheets, or in casts.
  • Dipstick: usually little/no blood or protein (low-grade proteinuria). beyond source Prerenal azotemia, by contrast, has a bland sediment (hyaline casts at most).
Muddy-brown granular casts — ATN

5. Urine Sediment & Renal Disease

Sediment = what's in the centrifuged pellet. The goal is localization: glomerulus, tubule, interstitium, or lower tract.

Cells

CellMeaning
RBC, isomorphicStone, tumor, infection, lower tract
RBC, dysmorphicGlomerular
Neutrophils (WBC)UTI; any tract inflammation
EosinophilsAcute interstitial nephritis (and some others)
Renal tubular epithelial (larger than WBC, central nucleus)Tubular injury / ATN
Urothelial (transitional)Renal pelvis to proximal urethra; round/triangular/pear-shaped; variable
Squamous (irregular, small central nucleus, abundant cytoplasm)Contamination (distal urethra/genital) → recollect
RTE cells (kidney), urothelial cells (pelvis to urethra), squamous cells (distal)

Casts

Casts are cylindrical molds of the renal tubule (protein matrix = Tamm-Horsfall + trapped material). A cast always means the material came from the kidney.

CastMeaning
RBC castGlomerulonephritis (glomerular bleeding)
WBC castIntrarenal inflammation: pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis
Granular / muddy-brownATN (tubular epithelial injury)
Fatty cast (oval fat bodies, "Maltese cross" under polarized light beyond source)Substantial glomerular protein loss: nephrotic syndrome (lipiduria)
Waxy / broad castAdvanced chronic kidney disease (stasis in dilated tubules)
Hyaline cast beyond sourceTamm-Horsfall only; normal, esp. concentrated urine/dehydration
RBC cast — pathognomonic for glomerulonephritis
How to read them Cells in the cast tell you the site: RBC = glomerulus; WBC = interstitium/pyelo; tubular cell (granular) = tubule; fat = nephrotic glomerulus; waxy/broad = chronic damage.

Free RBCs/WBCs without casts can come from anywhere in the tract; casts localize to the kidney.

Putting the sediment together

PatternTypical urinalysis / sedimentThink
NephriticHematuria, dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, variable (usually mild–moderate) proteinuriaImmune-mediated nephritis, RPGN, other glomerulonephritis
NephroticHeavy proteinuria (3–4+), hypoalbuminemia, edema, lipiduria, fatty casts, few cellsPodocyte/GBM disease
ATNMuddy-brown casts + RTE cells; SG fixed near isotonic beyond sourceIschemic/toxic tubular injury
Interstitial nephritisPyuria (WBC, eosinophils), WBC casts, mild protein; negative cultureDrugs, infection, autoimmune
PyelonephritisPyuria + bacteriuria, nitrite ±, WBC castsUpper tract infection
Cystitis / lower tractPyuria, bacteria, nitrite, no casts; isomorphic RBCsUTI, stones, tumor
Chronic kidney diseasePersistent albuminuria/proteinuria, waxy/broad casts, fixed SG; small echogenic kidneys on USAdvanced chronic disease
Prerenal azotemia beyond sourceBland sediment, hyaline casts, concentrated urineLow perfusion
ContaminatedMany squamous cells, mixed bacteriaRecollect clean-catch
Does it mean altered filtration, kidney damage, or structural disease? Filtration → SCr/eGFR. Damage → albuminuria/proteinuria, sediment findings, imaging. Structure → imaging (cysts, hydronephrosis, small echogenic kidneys). A patient can have damage with a normal eGFR (early diabetic kidney disease), or reduced eGFR with a bland urine (prerenal).

6. Renal Imaging: Choose by the Clinical Question

Clinical questionBest initial study
Possible obstruction / postrenal AKIRenal + bladder ultrasound (hydronephrosis)
Suspected stone, non-pregnant adultNoncontrast CT
Stone/obstruction in pregnancyUltrasound first (no radiation)
Characterize a renal mass (benign vs malignant, staging)Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI
Renal artery stenosisDuplex Doppler US, CT angiography, or MR angiography
Relative function of the two kidneysRadionuclide scan (e.g. before nephrectomy)

Ultrasound

  • Best test to rule out obstruction in AKI: dilated calyces (hydronephrosis, "bear claw"). Also evaluates masses, cysts (simple cyst vs mass/abscess), stones.
  • Polycystic kidney disease: multiple cysts. CKD: small, echogenic (scarred) kidneys vs normal/near-normal size in acute injury.
  • No radiation, no contrast → preferred in pregnancy.
Hydronephrosis (dilated calyces)
Chronic kidney disease (left, small echogenic) vs normal
ADPKD on ultrasound
ADPKD on CT

CT, MRI, nuclear

  • CT: stones (noncontrast), cysts, tumors and staging (a tumor doesn't enhance like normal kidney). Downsides: radiation and contrast nephrotoxicity in kidney disease.
  • MRI: high resolution for suspected renal cell carcinoma; MR angiography for renal artery stenosis.
  • Radionuclide scintigraphy: split (differential) function of the two kidneys.
CT: stone in the right proximal ureter
CT: renal cell carcinoma (non-enhancing mass)

7. Case BN & the Brick's Review Questions

CaseBN, 36 F, asymptomatic, BP 128/86, normal exam, no meds. Routine insurance labs: electrolytes normal, SCr 1.9 mg/dL (ref 0.6–1.4). What next?
Answer Repeat SCr (returned 2.0) and calculate eGFR (29 mL/min/1.73 m², about 1/3 of normal). Order urinalysis with microscopy (and quantify protein/albumin). Order renal ultrasound (obstruction, size, echogenicity, cysts). Nephrology referral for diagnosis and to slow progression. Kidney disease can be silent until late.

The Brick's three review questions are in the practice blocks at the end of §2 (muscle mass and SCr), §4 (dipstick in dysuria) and §6 (flank pain imaging).

8. Final High-Yield Table

TopicOne-liner
Early diseaseLower GFR (↑SCr/↓eGFR) or abnormal urine (protein, RBC, WBC, casts, crystals). UA + microscopy first, then imaging.
SCrMuscle-derived, freely filtered, ~10–15% secreted (overestimates GFR). Depends on muscle mass; use trends.
eGFR / CrCleGFR (CKD-EPI) = SCr + age + sex. CrCl = U×V/P (24-h; cumbersome; overestimates). Normal GFR ~120 at 20 y, −10/decade; quick = 140 − age.
BUN↑ with protein load, GI bleed, steroids, catabolism; ↓ with low protein, liver disease.
Dipstick bloodHeme only: RBC, Hb or myoglobin. Dysmorphic RBC = glomerular. RBC cast = GN.
Dipstick proteinAlbumin only (anionic). Misses light chains and microalbuminuria. 4+ = nephrotic range. Quantify with ACR/PCR.
LE / nitriteLE = WBCs (not necessarily infection). Nitrite = nitrate-reducing bacteria; negative doesn't exclude UTI (Enterococcus). WBC cast = kidney.
pHLow: extrarenal acidosis. High: vomiting/alkali, struvite (urease), distal RTA (alkaline despite acidosis).
SG1.008–1.009 isotonic (~280); <1.003 dilute; ~1.035 concentrated.
Glucose / ketones / bilirubinGlucose: filtered load > Tm (>~180 serum) or Fanconi. Ketones: acetoacetate (not reliably β-OHB). Bilirubin: conjugated; biliary obstruction/liver dz.
CrystalsCa oxalate = envelope; struvite = coffin lid (alkaline, Proteus); uric acid = rhomboid (acidic, gout/TLS); cystine = hexagon (cystinuria).
ATNMuddy-brown granular casts + RTE cells.
CastsRBC → GN; WBC → pyelo/AIN; granular → ATN; fatty → nephrotic; waxy/broad → advanced CKD.
ContaminationMany squamous cells → recollect clean-catch.
ImagingUS: obstruction, cysts, CKD (small echogenic); pregnancy. Noncontrast CT: stone. CT/MRI: mass. Doppler/CTA/MRA: RAS. Nuclear: split function.
